extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and readers of American government and foreign affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory textbook material describing the constitutional, institutional, and practical standards governing U.S. consular service, the treaty-making power, and related foreign policy doctrines (e.g., the Monroe Doctrine). Useful for learning what legal rules, customary practices, and functional duties shape U.S. foreign-affairs practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of consuls
rubrics_metrics.description: Consuls of all grades, like ambassadors, are appointed by the President with the approval of the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consular appointments include consuls-general-at-large, consuls-general, and consuls; vice-consuls and consular agents act under direction of the regular consul and (except for some vice-consuls/agents) appointments are subject to Senate ratification (see United States v. Eaton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and grading of consular service (1906 Act / merit system)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Act of 1906 reorganized the consular service, classifying and grading consuls so the President could extend the merit system to the branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Act, important vacancies are to be filled either by promotions of men whose ability has been tested in the service or by appointment of candidates who have passed oral and written examinations showing their fitness for the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for consuls
rubrics_metrics.description: Long experience; mastery of the language of the country; careful study of markets, export/import conditions, and trade opportunities; and some legal training are important qualifications for a consul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political service in an inland town or congressional district does not by itself qualify one for consular office. The passage notes a demand for higher standards and a move away from treating consular posts as political spoils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consular officer as commercial representative
rubrics_metrics.description: First and foremost the consular officer is a commercial representative who must certify invoices of goods intended for exportation and have wide knowledge of the character and value of goods produced for export in his district.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He must be master of tariff details to cooperate with U.S. customs officials in securing correct valuation and preventing smuggling; he must study local industrial and mercantile conditions, identify what the country needs, and report on ways American products could be made more marketable (form, packing, payment methods, etc.). The text also suggests appointing commercial attaches where government contracts are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consular duties relating to shipping and seamen
rubrics_metrics.description: Consuls have numerous duties concerning shipping and seamen: masters deposit ship registers with the consul when calling at a port and must secure return of papers before clearing; consuls may have jurisdiction over disputes among masters, officers, and men; may discharge seamen; hear complaints and give relief to distressed seamen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consuls are expected to make innumerable reports to the State Department which are edited and transmitted to the Department of Commerce for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consular administrative and judicial functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consuls administer oaths, take depositions, authenticate public documents, acknowledge deeds and other instruments, act as witnesses to marriages occurring in the consulate, and administer estates of U.S. citizens dying abroad under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consuls with salaries below $1,000 may undertake private business not conflicting with consular duties (acting then as private persons). In some states (e.g., historically China, Siam, Persia, Korea, Turkey) consuls exercised jurisdiction over American citizens in their districts—a practice rooted in differing legal systems and once abolished as local law westernized (e.g., Japan in 1899).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of consular powers: Consular Regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific powers and duties of consular officers are found in the 'Consular Regulations of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text treats these regulations as the primary articulation of consular authority and procedures for carrying out commercial, administrative, and protective functions abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making power (constitutional rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution provides that the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, two-thirds of the Senators present concurring, may make treaties; treaties so made shall stand with the Constitution and acts of Congress as the supreme law of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No express limitations are placed on the treaty-making power in the Constitution itself; this raises questions about the federal government's ability to make treaties concerning subjects normally within state control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jefferson's four limitations on treaty-making (normative rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thomas Jefferson laid down four rules: (1) treaties must concern foreign nations; (2) treaties should only cover subjects usually regulated by treaty and not otherwise regulable; (3) rights reserved to states must be excluded from treaty scope; (4) the President and Senate should not negotiate treaties on subjects of legislation in which the House of Representatives has constitutional participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of Jefferson's principles would greatly restrict federal treaty-making, but the text notes they have not been strictly followed in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial and practical treatment of treaty limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Jefferson's limitations exist as theory, courts and practice have often not recognized them: treaties affecting subjects ordinarily regulated by states have been held valid, and treaties have been used to assert rights (e.g., a foreign consul's claim to administer estates in a U.S. state).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives examples and notes debate over federal intervention in state criminal administration when treaty rights of foreigners are involved; Congress has not generally conferred federal jurisdiction for such matters despite suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties overlapping with congressional powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties may regulate matters that Congress could legislate—for example, commerce with foreign nations—so the President and Senate may make stipulations with foreign countries regulating such commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text underscores practical overlap between treaty obligations and domestic legislative authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies used to negotiate treaties; confirmation exception
rubrics_metrics.description: In negotiating treaties the President may employ the Secretary of State, an ambassador, a minister, a chargé d'affaires, or a private person; if a special agent is appointed, Senate confirmation is not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes executive flexibility in selecting negotiators and the constitutional/constitutional-practice distinction about confirmation of certain envoys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of Senate participation in negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the Senate may participate in the actual negotiation of treaties is unsettled: some assert the President may negotiate without Senate interference until presentation of the final document; others claim the Senate may share at any stage and even advise initiation of negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framers and Washington believed consultation with the Senate was appropriate; historical practice shows varying degrees of consultation by Presidents and Secretaries of State with influential Senators, especially members of the Senate foreign relations committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional initiation and advice on treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate sometimes seeks to initiate negotiations by resolution, and the House has, on occasions, attempted indirect participation (e.g., requesting papers). Congress has even passed acts advising the President on treaty terms (example: 1902 act advising terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the House has no constitutional share in treaty-making, both chambers have used resolutions and requests to influence negotiations; Presidents have sometimes complied with requests or consulted before negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate consideration, amendment, and ratification process
rubrics_metrics.description: When a treaty's terms are adjusted with the foreign power, the final draft is laid before the Senate, which may approve, amend, or reject it. Treaties are considered in executive session; when the Senate approves a treaty it is sent to the President for final exchange of ratifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice executive-session proceedings are often reported by the press. The President may refuse to exchange ratifications, thereby holding up a treaty even after Senate approval; if the Senate amends a treaty, the President must secure acceptance of changes by the foreign power. Completed treaties are made law by official proclamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential withholding of ratification after Senate approval
rubrics_metrics.description: The President has the power to refuse to exchange ratifications after Senate approval and thereby prevent a signed and approved treaty from going into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authority is justified on the ground that the President, through agents abroad, may have access to information unavailable to the Senate and may discover satisfactory reasons late in the process for not completing ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monroe Doctrine (practical principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Monroe Doctrine, as applied to Latin-American countries, broadly means the United States will oppose any European intervention aiming to extend their system to the Western Hemisphere, and that the American continents are no longer to be considered subjects for future colonization by European powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine developed under particular historical circumstances and has varied in form. Practically it came to mean the U.S. would respect existing European rights in the hemisphere but oppose intervention that would oppress or control the destiny of independent American states.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. engagement in world politics vs. 'splendid isolation' tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Although American tradition favored 'splendid isolation' from European political entanglements, commercial interests and protection of American trade have repeatedly drawn the United States into world politics and occasional military cooperation with other powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text provides historical examples (Barbary Wars, actions to protect commerce in China and Japan, participation in international conferences such as Berlin 1884, Algeciras 1906, Hague 1899 and 1907) and argues that commercial relations—not formal alliances—were the principal force linking the U.S. to world affairs.
